summary: Gives a brief overview of the North American Directory Forum's Standing Document series. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A short guide to the rule booklets of a group working on directories.

questions: what is the north american directory forum
what is the nadf public directory service
subtitle: A table of contents for the thirteen standing documents that let competing providers run one public X.500 directory.

tldr.problem: The North American Directory Forum (NADF) needs competing service providers to offer a cooperative Public Directory Service using the CCITT X.500 Recommendations.
tldr.mechanism: A series of numbered Standing Documents, SD-0 to SD-13, records the agreements. This memo summarizes each one and says how to obtain them.
tldr.outcome: The documents exist only in hardcopy and PostScript, so they cannot be distributed as RFCs. This memo obsoletes RFC 1417, 1295, 1255 and 1218.

today: RFC 1758 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1417, 1295, 1255 and 1218. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The NADF and Its Standing Documents
sections.content:
The North American Directory Forum is a collection of service providers that plans to cooperatively offer a Public Directory Service in North America using the CCITT X.500 Recommendations. It is unique among X.500 groups because it must achieve a cooperative service offered by competing providers.

The memo lists the standing documents from SD-0 (this overview) through SD-13 (accounting and settlements). SD-1 defines the scope of the NADF and SD-2 describes issues of interest. The rest describe agreements, and the NADF relies on X.500(88) as much as possible.
sections.eli5: Several rival companies want to share one directory, so they wrote a numbered set of agreements about how to do it.

sections.title: Naming and Mapping the Directory
sections.content:
SD-5 covers how a national authority should structure its DIT subtree and applies this to c=CA and c=US. The subtree is split into a public name-space, for entities with some public recognition such as states, counties and businesses, and several private name-spaces, each managed unilaterally by a public provider. Registration itself occurs outside the Directory. SD-6 gives guidelines for organizing a private name-space.

SD-7 covers mapping the DIT onto multiple DMDs. Because competing providers rule out a single owner of the public name-space, each provider links from it into its own private name-space, and a central authority called the CAN publishes a roadmap. SD-12 is a registry of ADDMD names.
sections.eli5: There is a shared public part of the phone book and private parts each company looks after, with a central map showing how they connect.

sections.title: Service, Pilot, Security and Accounting
sections.content:
SD-3 holds agreements about the Directory service, such as quality of service, and SD-4 about the Directory schema. SD-8 describes the agreements for the NADF Pilot, and SD-9 the charter and procedures of the Central Administration.

SD-10 gives the policy on security and privacy, and its Attachment 1 is a User Bill of Rights for entries and listings in the Public Directory. SD-11 describes the security facilities of the Directory and the mechanisms the Public Directory will use. SD-13 gives a model and principles for accounting and settlement.
sections.eli5: Other booklets cover how good the service must be, a trial run, keeping information safe, and how companies pay each other.

sections.title: Getting the Documents
sections.content: The standing documents are available only in hardcopy and PostScript form. Since they do not exist in ASCII, they cannot be distributed as informational RFCs. Hardcopies come from the NADF Secretariat in Washington, DC, and PostScript files (sd-*.ps) from an anonymous FTP area. The memo says security issues are not discussed in it.
sections.eli5: The booklets could not be printed in the RFC series, so you had to get them by mail or download them separately.
